accroche: The prime suspect spends six days in prison. His name is Guillaume Apollinaire, and he had nothing to do with it.
contenu_vulgarise:
On Monday, August 21, 1911, the Louvre's weekly closing day, a man in a work smock walks into the museum. Vincenzo Peruggia is a glazier; he once fitted the *Mona Lisa*'s protective glass. He waits until he is alone in the Salon Carré, takes the painting off the wall, strips it of its frame in a stairwell, and walks out with the canvas, likely hidden under his clothes. No one notices anything. The theft is not discovered until the next morning.

The investigation goes astray almost at once, and that is where the story turns unexpected.

## The investigation

A few years earlier, a Belgian adventurer, Géry Pieret, had stolen Iberian statuettes from the Louvre, then sold two of them to a young painter still little known, Pablo Picasso. Pieret had also been the secretary of a poet, Guillaume Apollinaire, who had known him since 1905 and occasionally put him up.

When the police, looking for a culprit for the theft of the *Mona Lisa*, pick up the trail of those earlier thefts, suspicion falls on this circle. Apollinaire is arrested and jailed at the Santé Prison on September 7, 1911; he is released six days later, on September 12, on provisional release. Picasso is questioned in turn, terrified at the thought of being expelled from France. Neither has the slightest connection to the theft of the painting: they are released, the statuette case handled separately, with no established link to the disappearance of the *Mona Lisa*.

Meanwhile, Peruggia keeps the canvas for two years in his Paris room, on the rue de l'Hôpital-Saint-Louis, in the false bottom of a suitcase. An inspector comes to question him as early as September 29, 1911, without searching the room: no one imagines that a humble workman could have committed such a theft.

Peruggia gives himself away. Convinced that the work belongs to Italy, he returns to Florence with the painting and shows it, on December 10, 1913, to the antiques dealer Alfredo Geri, hoping for a reward. Geri has the canvas authenticated by the director of the Uffizi Gallery, alerts the police, and Peruggia is arrested at his hotel. He gets a light sentence, one year reduced to seven months.

## What this shifts

The *Mona Lisa* returns to the Louvre in early 1914, after a farewell tour across Italy. A lasting irony: during the two years of its absence, the empty spot on the wall draws more visitors than the painting had drawn before. The theft did not merely make a work disappear; through the media coverage of the affair and its false culprits, it made it more famous than it had ever been.

repere.texte: Peruggia is first questioned at his home on September 29, 1911, less than six weeks after the theft, without his room being searched. The *Mona Lisa* will stay hidden there for nearly two more years, until he himself tries to resell it in Florence on December 10, 1913.

carte.punch: The prime suspect is named Guillaume Apollinaire, and he had nothing to do with it.
carte.idee: In 1911, a glazier takes the *Mona Lisa* off the Louvre wall and hides it for two years in his room. The investigation first arrests Apollinaire and questions Picasso, both innocent. The thief gives himself away in 1913 by trying to resell the canvas in Florence.

quiz.question: Why does the investigation into the theft of the *Mona Lisa* first turn to Guillaume Apollinaire and Pablo Picasso?
choix: Because a witness claimed to have seen them lurking near the Louvre on the very day of the theft
Because they had publicly criticized the way the Louvre preserved its works
Because of a separate case of statuettes stolen by a former secretary of Apollinaire's and resold to Picasso
Because Peruggia himself had named them to divert suspicion from himself
quiz.explication: The link lies in an earlier case unrelated to the theft of the *Mona Lisa*: Géry Pieret, Apollinaire's former occasional secretary, had stolen Iberian statuettes from the Louvre and sold two of them to Picasso. It is that case of handling stolen goods that puts the two men in the spotlight, not the slightest clue tying them to the theft of the painting itself.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happens, ironically, during the two years the *Mona Lisa* is absent from the Louvre?
choix: The Louvre temporarily closes the Salon Carré to the public
The empty spot on the wall draws more visitors than the painting had drawn before
A copy is displayed in its place without anyone noticing
The museum receives an offer to sell the spot outright
quiz_supplementaire.explication: During the two years the *Mona Lisa* is gone, the empty spot draws more visitors than the painting drew before the theft, the media coverage of the affair having made the work more famous.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does Peruggia end up getting arrested, two years after the theft?
choix: A neighbor reports him after spotting the canvas in his room
The police find his fingerprints on the discarded frame
He tries to resell the painting to a Florence antiques dealer, who alerts the police
He is arrested trying to leave France with the canvas
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Convinced that the work belongs to Italy, Peruggia shows it on December 10, 1913 to the antiques dealer Alfredo Geri in Florence, hoping for a reward; Geri has the canvas authenticated and alerts the police.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What connection did Vincenzo Peruggia have to the *Mona Lisa* before stealing it?
choix: He was a night guard at the Louvre's Salon Carré
He had restored the painting's frame a few years earlier
He had already tried to steal the painting once before, in 1909
He had once installed the painting's protective glass, as a glazier
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Peruggia is a glazier by trade and had once installed the *Mona Lisa*'s protective glass, which gave him knowledge of the painting's security setup.
